📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.
  • And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
  • Tesla’s official Robotaxi account revealed the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account revealed the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

According to recent reports, the order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

In a recent development, the subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print notes “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and notes you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Sources indicate that tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla claims they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

In a recent development, no point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a upcoming two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

Sources indicate that if you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. A Complete Guide to Caring For Your Nails While Working Out

💡 Key Takeaways

  • THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat. The one area where a sweat session can fall short, however, is when it comes to the health of our nails.

Recent findings suggest that if you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym. Between chipped polish, cracks and peeling, and the mental gymnastics of trying to avoid both, it can sometimes feel like your nails (and your sanity) are getting a workout of their own. “When I’m lifting plates or handling weights, I’m always conscious of how I’m gripping,” shares celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador Gina Edwards, who's a frequent gym-goer herself. “I use my finger pads rather than the tips of my fingers to help avoid putting unnecessary pressure on my nails.”.

Industry observers note that meet the experts: Gina Edwards is a celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador. Dana Stern, MD, is a Upcoming York-based dermatologist who specializes in nail disorders. Marisa Garshick, MD, is a dermatologist based in New York City. Jin Soon Choi is a celebrity manicurist in New York City.

In a recent development, not into manicures? Unfortunately, that doesn't mean you're completely off the hook. Even bare nails can take a beating: “The nail is a thousand times more absorptive of water than the skin,” says New York dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, who specializes in nail disorders. And because frequent handwashing and exposure to moisture often go hand in hand with working out, nails are subjected to expansion as they absorb water and contraction as they dry. “Repeated wet-dry cycles can contribute to splitting and peeling, particularly in people already prone to brittle nails,” Dr Stern adds.

But not to worry—you don’t have to choose between having polished digits and getting your fitness on. With a few smart habits, you can avoid all the pitfalls. Here’s how.

No matter how you choose to work out, there are plenty of ways your nails can suffer. And most of us don't even realize we're putting them in harm's way until it's too late. Maybe you're in a workout class, engaging in some friendly competition with your neighbor to see who can knock out their burpees the fastest, only to jam a nail as your hands hit the ground. Or perhaps the damage happens before you even break a sweat. Picture it: You're pulling on your most compressive pair of leggings when a nail snags on the fabric or, worse, bends backward and breaks.

It has been revealed that of course, some activities pose a more obvious risk than others. Exercises that involve “repetitive gripping, pressure, or friction, such as weightlifting, rock climbing, and certain types of strength training” can be especially hard on your nails, says Marisa Garshick, MD, a dermatologist based in New York City.

Here are a few of the ways your workout routine might be doing a number on them:.

Handling dumbbells, weight plates, and other equipment can put pressure on nails, especially if they're long, dry, or already weak, says celebrity manicurist Jin Soon Choi.

Jamming a nail against a hard surface or repeatedly putting pressure on it can cause the nail plate to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis. This can happen to natural nails, too, although extensions may create additional opportunities for snagging.

In a recent development, when a falsie gets caught on something, it can even cause the underlying natural nail to lift from the nail bed, explains Dr. Stern. Depending on the extent of the damage, it can take months for a healthy newly introduced nail to grow in.

Frequent handwashing and exposure to harsh cleansers (including those used to wipe down gym equipment and alcohol-based hand sanitizers) can contribute to splitting and peeling, Dr. Stern adds.

While running and cycling may be gentler on your hands, repeated pressure inside athletic shoes can cause bruising beneath the nail (known as a subungual hematoma), thickening, or even nail loss, explains Dr. Garshick.

Industry observers note that the good news? Most workout-related nail damage is temporary, provided the nail matrix, which is responsible for nail growth, hasn't been damaged. But more serious injuries can have lasting consequences. A crush injury—heavy weight falling on a nail, for example—could cause permanent damage to the nail matrix, Dr. Stern claims. Even when the damage isn't permanent, patience is key. According to Dr. Garshick, fingernails typically take three to six months to grow out, while toenails can take twelve to eighteen months.

In a recent development, the goal isn't to give up your favorite workouts or your favorite manicures. A few tweaks to your nail-care routine and how you handle equipment can make all the difference.

Here's what the pros recommend to keep your nails looking and feeling their best.

This ultra-nourishing product delivers a healthy dose of barrier-repairing ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide sans greasy residue.

Jinsoon Primrose + Honeysuckle Healing Cuticle Oil.

Choi recommends this product, from her own line, before bed to help maintain healthy nails and cuticles.

OPI Repair Mode Bond Building Nail Serum.

Sources indicate that you’ve heard of bond builders for hair, right? This is the same thing, but for nails. It promises longer, stronger nails in just four weeks.

Recent findings suggest that it’s crucial to keep in mind that Dr. Garshick states not every nail change is workout-related. Persistent discoloration, thickening, or lifting can sometimes indicate a fungal infection, psoriasis, or another nail condition. A latest or changing dark streak, particularly one that doesn't grow out, should also be evaluated by a board-certified dermatologist.

At the end of the day, you don't have to choose between crushing your fitness goals and keeping your nails in good shape. In fact, Choi points out that exercise itself can actually be beneficial for nail health, as physical activity promotes healthy circulation, helping deliver oxygen and nutrients to the tissues responsible for nail growth.

It's the accidental injuries and repeated pressure that can cause problems, not the workouts themselves. With a few simple adjustments to your nail-care routine and a bit more awareness of how you're handling equipment, you can keep breaking a sweat without breaking a nail.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging.
  • Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has rapidly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a significant difference.
  • When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has rapidly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a significant difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Recent findings suggest that instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

Industry observers note that if I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be rapidly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It has been revealed that it may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

It has been revealed that and that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as promptly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

According to recent reports, USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road rapidly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

In a recent development, for years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested.
  • And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
  • The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the organization started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the organization started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make right now, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

In a recent development, yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

In a recent development, tesla’s answer to all those owners is a fresh car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

According to recent reports, you don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

In a recent development, and the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no newly introduced revenue attached.

A upcoming vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym.
  • As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.
  • Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

“It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”.

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” notes Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, indicates Carr.

In a recent development, “They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly vital, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” says Carr.

It has been revealed that picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”.

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

Recent findings suggest that “They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” says Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”.

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” says Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”.

Kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

Industry observers note that the Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

Recent findings suggest that “We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” remarked Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”.

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

It has been revealed that previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

It has been revealed that this was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

In a recent development, they measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

In a recent development, when the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is notable to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” remarked Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Sources indicate that judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more crucial to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She remarked that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is vital to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

Industry observers note that “I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” stated Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ fresh electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

In a recent development, originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

According to recent reports, in other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

In a recent development, to be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

In a recent development, there are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis aims to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a newly introduced Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

SOURCE: Stellantis, via Mopar Insiders.

#121639. How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2198 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay.
  • Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture.
  • Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

Sources indicate that the exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” states Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

In the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, notes physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

It has been revealed that the term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” says Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”.

In the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” claims Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” claims Ritchey.

Industry observers note that if you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Industry observers note that girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she states.

Sources indicate that there's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she says. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own plans for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”.

According to recent reports, if you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

According to recent reports, according to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” states Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”.

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

Ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she says. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”.

It’s key to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

That’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”.

Industry observers note that in other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

According to recent reports, what’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

It has been revealed that “It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey notes. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”.

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

Beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”.

Recent findings suggest that of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” says Girard.

Recent findings suggest that so if you’ve been curious to try a new sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”.

Recent findings suggest that as the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most vital ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” states Ritchey.

According to recent reports, have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The important thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” states Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

Recent findings suggest that they can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she says. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”.

Appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the Newly introduced School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

💡 Key Takeaways

  • When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its newly introduced NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The tech giant’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The upcoming Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The latest NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

According to recent reports, on top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Sources indicate that power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the latest NX7 in the comments, today.

Breaking: A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?
  • A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.
  • Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

Sources indicate that A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

Recent findings suggest that “Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”.

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

In a recent development, additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”.

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

It has been revealed that “A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein mentioned. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”.

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein noted.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”.

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

In a recent development, “For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein mentioned. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”.

It has been revealed that sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

Sources indicate that “I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein stated. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority.
  • Protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority. The reason isn’t quantum computers.

Protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters. The quantum threat has always been a hardware problem, and hardware problems announce themselves years in advance because somebody has to build the machine. The AI version is a math problem. A sufficiently capable model could find a structural shortcut in the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin, and it would need no special hardware to do it.

Sources indicate that researcher Justin Drake raised the scenario in October. In a worst case, he said, existing signatures could become vulnerable within months.

An Anthropic mathematician named Levent Alpöge posted a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with an unreleased version of Claude, along with a formalized proof archive. Nobody has verified it. It doesn’t break elliptic curve cryptography and nobody is claiming it does. What it does is demonstrate the capability class Drake was describing, roughly a month after he described it.

Sources indicate that axios reported Tuesday that more than two dozen people familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic say employees worry their most advanced unreleased models may never be safe enough to release. The concerns named include reward hacking, models that hide or misrepresent their reasoning, and systems capable enough to find weaknesses in the safety measures their own developers built. OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed Sunday that labs agree on shared limits on how far they train models.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The proposal replaces elliptic curves with hash-based cryptography, which rests on fewer structural assumptions about mathematics. It touches how people authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how layer-2 data gets verified. Drake proposed pulling the deadline from December 2029 to December 2028. Ethlabs withdrew its faster-block-production proposal from the Hegotá upgrade to free up engineers. The Foundation has deployed AI agents to hunt bugs in its own infrastructure, which is a reasonable response and also an admission about where the advantage presently sits.

Wedderburn’s own framing: it’s harder than the Merge, and there’s less time. He also acknowledged that moving faster makes it easier to ship bugs.

Sources indicate that bitcoin is on the same road. Blockstream’s Jonas Nick published a security analysis of SHRINCS last week, the apparent frontrunner to replace Bitcoin’s signatures, with sizes running from 548 bytes to 5,777 against today’s 64 to 71.

In a recent development, so the AI threat is looming (and accelerating), but the two largest crypto assets have teams that are responding. Now we wait on action, and more assurances that crypto is safe from AI threats. Assurances that could ensure the bottom is in fact in, if and when they arrive….

China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • Industry observers note that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight.
  • In a recent development, the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC notes every system worked normally.

Industry observers note that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

In a recent development, the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

Sources indicate that the program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

According to recent reports, the obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and mentioned it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither firm has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

Industry observers note that COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, Latest York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Sources indicate that heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

Industry observers note that for years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

Recent findings suggest that and this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

In a recent development, china also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

If you’re following the electrification of transport, the cheapest place to start is your own roof: home solar can power your EV for close to nothing. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs.
